analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Secretary, you may resume. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. Just before we broke for the recess, I was talking about Chapter 11A of the Code of West Virginia. Article 4 of that chapter provides for the sale of lands by a deputy commissioner. Section 12 of Article 4 is where I find my first major point. Section 12 provides that in the suit that is brought, notice to former owners, interested parties, is given by publication only. It makes it clear, makes it explicit, that it is the intent and will of the legislature that publication is all that is required and all that is necessary. I feel strongly that that is a denial of due process under the 14th Amendment to the Constitution of the United States. My second point is in Article 3, which is the article where the sheriff sells. And if you'll recall, after the sheriff sells to the state, there is a period of 18 months to redeem. I say that if that 18-month period for redemption is used as a statute of limitations to bar the owner from asserting rights that were denied him by Point 1, then that also is a violation of due process of law. If I can look... Is that because there's nothing to trigger the 18 months? Exactly, Your Honor. The statute runs before the right has accrued. Of course, on that theory, then, no notice by publication is without infirmity. Isn't that true? No notice. Beg your pardon, sir? Notices by publication are then constitutionally doubtful, aren't they? I agree. In all cases. Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Absolutely. Absolutely. The opinion in the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, I think, shows clearly what I'm driving at. First of all, he takes up my Point 1 and talks about denial of due process because of no personal service of notice by publication only. He cites State Against Simmons, an old West Virginia case, not so old, 1951, which laid down the law at that time that, in West Virginia, personal notice was not required, the publication was sufficient. And on that reasoning, he quotes syllabus 1 of State Against Simmons and says that is the law at that time. Then he goes into the famous case of Mullane against Central Hanover Bank and Trust Company and the cases that followed it, and he talks about them. And he says, he begins to say, this is the developing of a new approach to due process. And he quotes with approval from the Mullane case, to the extent notice reasonably calculated to apprise interested parties. At that point, it looks like I'm going to get somewhere with this opinion. And then, then, it deviates. He cites Fuentes against Simmons, decided by this case, this court, pardon me, in 1972. Actually, as you will recall, that case really held that the Florida and Pennsylvania Replevin statutes were invalid because they provided for seizure of personal property without notice. But in the language in that opinion, the court stated that not only does due process protect absolute ownership, but it protects, and here's the key words, significant property interests and statutory entitlements. And then, then, then, the opinion seizes on 11A38, which is the 18-month period, and says that since the property was not redeemed in 18 months, the owner, the former owner, no longer had a significant property interest. Therefore, it was not entitled to due process or notice, personal notice. He calls the 18-month period a statutory entitlement, which he says is lost when the time expires. And in my humble opinion, the, the, the, the, the court's opinion goes full cycle. He, uh, he uses 11A38 as a statute of limitations to bar what he was about to admit was an unconstitutional denial of due process. Do you think the state had a right to put any limitation on it? Of course, Your Honor. Uh, the, the 18-month period was, was a period of, of redemption. And, that's all. It was just a waiting period, in my opinion. Do you think that you could come in 50 years later and claim it? Well, it would depend, Your Honor, on, on... Do you? In this case, do you think so? No, sir. Yes, yes. If there, if there, if there was a denial of due process and it was not cured by some other means, I would say yes. Well, then that, you just, you just say that you can't publish. Right? I said that publication is not good service. Under any circumstances. Yes, yes. Well, what do you worry about, 11 months or anything else? I don't worry about it, but the, but the, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, Your Honor, used that to bar the right to assail the, the lack of due process. Well, I, I don't understand what you're complaining. Your complaint is that, under no circumstances can you take anybody's property without personal service. Yes, sir. If the service is, I think, I think... If the person, if the owner happens to be in Russia, you would serve him how? Oh, no, no, no, Your Honor. I think process should issue. I, I, I didn't make myself clear. A suit should be started like any lawsuit. Process should issue. It should be served on all parties who can be found. If they cannot be found, then I say publication is fine. And how could this person be found? The owner was whom? Mrs. Cecil G. Pearson. She was the owner. Who was the owner of record? She was the owner of record, Your Honor. She, her name was not on the, on the assessment roll. It was in the name of a former owner on the assessment, in the assessor's office. But she was the owner and her deed was of record. Well, suppose he'd go to the assessment record and he sent a notice to that person. Would that be all right? And it so happens that it belongs to the man in Russia. Your Honor, I don't say the due process is an absolute guarantee of notice. I say that a suit should be started and process issued, reasonably calculated, to, to reach the interested parties. If they cannot be found, then they have had due process. That's my point. Why isn't that this case? No, sir, because no process was ever issued. It was publication only. There was no, no summons issued. What could this, what do you think, what should the state have done? The state should have started a suit the way any other suit has started. By filing a complaint and having the clerk issue process delivered to a deputy sheriff and having go out to serve the parties. Who would the defendants have been in this suit? The defendants in the suit as it is now are the former property owners. Well, the state had no record of Mrs. Pearson's ownership other than in the deed book. Your Honor, my answer to that would be that if process had issued and the sheriff had gone out looking for H.C. Pearson Jr., he might have found out that he was deceased. He might have found Mrs. Pearson. But whether he found her or not, the fact that he tried, she would have had due process. That is my, that is my feeling. You don't argue that they, that the, that all the state had to do was to look in the, in the deed records of the county? Yes, sir. I think that's a valid point. I'm not saying that they have to do that, but I think if they had looked, they could have found it. Well, most purchasers will certainly look at the, certainly, look at the title of the property. Yes, Your Honor. Yes, Your Honor. I can't, I can't say what the standard must be. Under Mullane, it says reasonable notice. All the cases you rely on, though, so far as what kind of notice you get, involve unexpected potential for deprivation. That is, condemnation, something like that. They don't involve the annual recurring payment of taxes that everybody expects to have to pay on their property. That is, that is true, Your Honor. But I, but I, I maintain the due process goes to protect the little man whose property is lost because he fails to pay his taxes. Well, wouldn't it be any different if this were the local bank type? Would your principles any different if the local bank was in the posture of your client? No, sir. Same, same. Well, you said the little people and you were talking about. Because the local bank is probably going to pay us taxes. Well, but probably, in the same posture, they didn't pay their taxes because of the oversight of a clerk. In that case, no, I don't find any difference, no, sir. Or whether they're senile makes no difference. Or whether they're 21 years old or 31 and very alert, does it really? Not, sir. No, sir, not really. Is it possible that Jeff Klein didn't get interested in this whole business until they started drilling for gas? Certainly, Your Honor. I don't deny that. But the stakes have got to be high to enable a little person to be able to come up to this court. There's no use trying to hide that fact. She came to her attorney, and he advised her what to do. And that's true. If the land were of no value, she wouldn't be here. And that's why it hasn't come up for 10 years. The taxes failed to be paid in 1961. And in 67, I believe it was, it was sold to W.P. Dodd. So six years, there's no interest. That's right. Well, there probably wouldn't have been any tax bills after the property became the, the real estate became the property of the state, was there? Well, in West Virginia, the assessor actually is not required to send out bills that he does in Kanawha County now. And I expect he was doing it then. But it's purely a matter of convenience to the property. But after the property, after the real estate became the property of the state... No, that's quite right. Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honor. There was nobody to send a bill to. Exactly. There was no private owner. No, sir. Is that right? Yes, sir. Well, I've interrupted you. Let me ask you this. It's far from clear to me. There were two, at least two separate proceedings here. One was after the taxes were not paid in 1961, then at the sheriff's sale, there being no bidders, the property became, the real estate became the property of the state. Yes, sir. And there was no notice of that. Oh, no. To anybody. No, sir. Now, is that the... And then later, and then later, the state conveyed the property to somebody else, correct? Yes, sir. Now, which of those two transactions, of which, of neither of which was notice given, personal notice given, are you complaining of? The second one. The second one, Your Honor. Not the first one, sir? No, not really. Why not? Well, because the Dodd title is not derived from the sheriff's sale. The only thing the sheriff's... That's the way the Dodd... That's the way your title was taken away. Well, actually... It was by the sale of the state, and you no longer owned it. The state did. We had a right to redeem, Your Honor. Yes, but you were given no notice of that transfer to the state. You were given no notice of your 18-month period to redeem, and you're not complaining about that. Is that right? I'm complaining about it being used as a statute of limitations. Why aren't you complaining about that substantively, per seat? I... Because I don't think it's an issue in this case. Well, it's a very big part of the proceedings. It ended up with a real estate belonging to somebody else, didn't it? It went first to the state, didn't it? Yes, Your Honor. Yes, Your Honor. Without any notice. Right. And you're not complaining of that? Well, I could complain about that, but I think you could. Well, I know you could, but are you? No, sir. All right. Well, doesn't your 18 months run from that event? Yes, sir. Later on. Yes, sir. That's right. I'm complaining... I don't know how you upset the statute of limitations. The statute of limitations of ruling without getting to the first sale. Your Honor, the first sale simply starts the statute... You challenge it in your complaint or in your... Whatever filing... As I read the... As I read this, you challenge the... Well, I... The initial sale, you challenge it. It... It wasn't good notice, but the dot title depends on the second sale, and that's why I'm challenging... The second sale by somebody else, by the state who had acquired it as a result of this sheriff's transfer to the sale... To the state. That's what deprived you, your client, of its property. Well... If the second sale... If the state got good title to the property out of the first sale, there's nothing wrong with the second sale. That's right. No, sir. I don't see it that way. I'm sorry. The due process issue, I think, arises out of the deputy commissioner's sale. Well, the sheriff's sale simply started the running of the 18-month period, which is used... The Supreme Court of West Virginia seized upon that... Yes, sir. ...that put the nail in your coffin. That's right. Yes, sir. The 18 months, it called it a statute of limitations, which had run before the right had occurred to... Excuse me. Go ahead, sir. No, you're right now. Pardon me. Well, I'll finish it. The 18-month period had expired before the right to challenge due process in the deputy commissioner's sale had even accrued. And that is my position. Well, then, is your position, at least in part, that the privilege of redemption that's given to you in the second sale is the kind of entitlement of which the state has to give you notice if it's going to take you away from you? Now, Your Honor, I don't follow that. But in the second sale, the only redemption possible... There is no redemption after that second sale. Well, but I mean, at the second sale, you have... Isn't that the one where the West Virginia Supreme Court talks about the privilege of redemption? It has run out by then. Therefore, you have no significant property interest, and therefore you're not entitled to due process in the deputy commissioner's suit. Well, there were two things that extinguished your client's title. The first was the sheriff's process. Yes, sir. And that triggered the commencement of the 18-month redemption period. And then the final mail in the coffin, to borrow that phrase, was the expiration of the redemption period. Is that not so? Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honor. But they were both involved, were they not? They were both involved, and the first one wasn't good, granted. I'll be willing to attack it, but I don't think that's an issue in this case. That's not the way we see it. Well, if that's not an issue, and if that was perfectly constitutional, then this real estate in question was the property of the state at the time that it was conveyed to the other party. And you had no standing to complain about it. I think I did, Your Honor. I mean, and that's really, in effect, what the Supreme Court of your state held. But it didn't go back to any denial of notice at the time the property, the real estate, became the property of the state. Yes, sir. But you're not attacking that here. You're assuming the constitutionality of that transfer. Well, I don't think it's... It's not an issue in the lawsuit that was brought to sell the property. The only issue there was the state is selling property, and the former owner should have notice. And he didn't get it. Well, how do you share it? I thought that your claim was that the former owner should have had notice before the property invested in the state. And if you concede that that transfer of property to the state was wholly valid, then I fail to see why the state couldn't do with the property what it wished without any notice to anybody, any landlord. Well? Mr. Terry, with regard to the first sale, does the record tell us whether or not your client had notice of that sale? Yeah, okay. I don't think it would be done. There was no notice of that sale. Does the record show that? I don't know. No, I don't know what does it not, your honor. But under the law, all the sheriff does is publish. So it would be no better than the second one. But it would be consistent with the record that she might have read the newspaper, been told by somebody, and said, well, I don't care because the land's worthless. That's possible, I suppose. Of course it's possible, your honor. Yes, sir. Your honor, I may have a few minutes left. May I reserve my time? Very well. Mr. Rice. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. Basically, my profession as a lawyer is a title attorney. That's about all I do. And I am astounded that a title matter of this nature would bring me before this court. Nevertheless, perhaps I can shed some light on the subject because I have been in it from the very beginning. It's important for this court to know who H.C. Pearson Sr. was. That is the man, the husband of the appellant, now deceased. That is the husband is now deceased. And his son was H.C. Pearson Jr. But in the discovery deposition of H.C. Pearson Sr., we asked him to give us some of his previous job experience. That man was 84 years old at the time, which was 1968. And he said, I spent almost 16 years with Ohio Fuel Gas Company, which was a predecessor company to my present employer. And the question was, in what capacity? And the answer was, as engineer and land department man. I had charge of both of those departments for at least 12 years. He left Ohio Fuel in 1927. And we asked him what his experience in oil and gas work was from 1927 up until the present time. And he said, I own some properties, oil and gas properties in Kentucky and some in West Virginia. And I have helped drill several wells with your company. And we asked him, did he own some tracts of land? And he said, well, a few years ago, I expect I had 50, 60, or 70 tracts. But I sold most of my tracts in Jackson County to Star Gas Company, et cetera. The record in this case will show that the appellant and her husband, who handled the tax tickets for her, were knowledgeable people. They knew the tax deed procedure in West Virginia. They knew the taxing system for real property taxes in West Virginia. It's helpful to keep the facts in a proper chronological order. Well, those elements would only relate to some equitable aspect rather than a due process, would they not? I think they may impinge on both of them. Certainly equitable. At least equitable, yes. Well, do you give a different due process for knowledgeable people than you do to less knowledgeable people? No, but I think it's helpful to understand who the man was. Now, the tax ticket, after H.C. Pearson, Jr. had conveyed the tract of land, the undivided mineral interest to his mother in 1937, stayed in the son's name. And the mother and father either picked up that tax ticket, or if it was mailed to them, they paid that tax ticket in the son's name. In what year? In 1937. They paid the tax ticket that way for 24 years. From 1937, when they bought it. From 61. W.H. Odell up until 1961. Then in 1961, that tax ticket did not get paid. And in 1962, there was a proceeding with two publications in two local newspapers that said that that tract of land would be sold to the state of West Virginia if it were not redeemed. And then it was, then the sale occurred, and at this sale, individual bidders can come in and bid at least the amount of the taxes. And if they do, then that tract of land will be, or parcel or interest, will be sold to the individual purchaser. And there is a notice provision in that statute, a personal notice provision. Before you can get a county clerk's tax deed pursuant to that sale, there is personal notice. But if these tracts of land, because of the minuscule amount of interest and the time and expense that it takes to check the title to find out who the owners are and where they are and how to serve them, people won't bid them in at the sheriff's sale. They won't bid on the tracts of land and own them and pay the taxes, and the former owner quite obviously won't pay the taxes. So you come up to the sale in 1965. Mr. Rice, before you get to 65, does the record tell us whether, in fact, the appellant got personal notice in 62? You say the statute requires it, is that right? The statute would have required it had there been an individual purchaser who had bid the amount of the taxes. In this case, that did not happen. Thus, the land went to the state for the amount of the taxes. With no personal notice. With no personal notice. Either required or given. That's right. Or published. No, there was publication, yes. All right. Now, do you defend, if that transaction were here on its merits, would you defend that? I take it the Supreme Court of West Virginia did not say that that transaction would survive due process analysis. I would defend it, Your Honor. But the Supreme Court of West Virginia did. It said that it was immune because of the statute of limitations. Well, you see, you have to keep the sheriff's sale first in the point of time. And that one has a publication. And I would defend that from a matter of due process. The Supreme Court of West Virginia. Sir? What about the Supreme Court of West Virginia? The Supreme Court of West Virginia would have to hold. Well, they said that 18 months then went by and cured any defects. Or at least it shielded that transaction. Because that is a constitutional provision in West Virginia. The Constitution of 1872 says that if the taxes are not paid and they remain unredeemed for 18 months, the title vests in the state of West Virginia. We may as well face it. That's what the Constitution says. But if there had been a sale to a private party at the auction, personal notice would have been given, would have been required, would it not, to the former owner? In order for the purchaser who bid it in, that would be required. Personal notice and then a period for an opportunity to redeem. Yes. Correct? Yes. But since there was no such private purchaser, and instead the title went to the state, no personal notice required or given. That's right. That's right. And there wasn't any judicial proceeding, was there? There was not. And the statute doesn't require one? It's simply a transfer of title. It's a forfeiture. A taking of property. Mr. Justice Stewart, that is right. And after 18 months, it's final. That is what the statute said, and that's what the Constitution of 1872 says. Mr. Rice, is there any difference in the character of the title which a private purchaser in 1962, and we're still focusing on the first transaction, would have received after getting personal notice, and the character of the title the state got without any such personal notice? Are both of them subject to an 18-month period of redemption by the former owner? No. No. Once the individual purchaser has to wait 18 months in order to get an abstract of title and a survey made, so that the periods are roughly the same time. But before the 18-month starts to run, in the event that a private person buys at the auction, then the former owner gets personal notice. That's right. But when the sale is to the state, no such notice. Why the difference? Mr. Justice Stevens, the reason is the expense. Quite obviously, the tract of land is not valuable enough, or may not be valuable enough, for the owner to pay the taxes. And thus you come to a place, whether you're going to spend $50 an hour for a title examining attorney, to determine who the owners are, who the true owners are, and where they are. I see. And you presume it's worth the trouble if somebody's willing to pay for the property, and if they're not, it's not worth the money. That's the thought. Yes. May I ask one other question before you go on? The state of West Virginia has filed an amicus brief in support of your position, in which they say, on page two in the summary of the argument, that if the appellant had made any attempt to pay her taxes for a period of almost four and a half years, she would have learned of the tax status of the property and could have effected redemption. They seem to assume that she had a four and a half year period in which to redeem. Do you agree with that? No. Rather than the 18 months. I do not agree with it. However, I did not write that name. It misunderstands its own statutes, I guess. I see. Well, isn't it true that even after the 18 months under Section 11A-4-18, Ms. Pearson had a right to apply to a state court for permission to redeem her property, and that could have been granted? Mr. Justice Stewart, she was entitled by grace of the legislature to do that. And by grace in the discretion of a court, of a court, to your permission. Correct. Yes. So it wasn't an absolute foreclosure. I mean, she did have that possibility open to her. By the grace of the legislature. And did she, in fact, make an unsuccessful attempt to redeem under that same location? Oh, no. No, she never attempted to redeem the property until... You see, once she discovered that the property had been sold to W.P. Dodd in late 1967, even then she didn't go try to pay her taxes. She waited until the gas well came in and produced an open flow of 100 million cubic feet a day, and then went to the state of West Virginia and attempted to get a certificate of redemption. Waited until the race was over and then went and bought a ticket on the winner. Yes. One more question, if I may, Mr. Rice. After the 18-month period runs, and prior to the sale pursuant to publication, as I understand the West Virginia Court, there is no right in the former owner to have the property redeemed. But there is a provision that the court may, in its discretion, allow it to be done. Is there any guideline whatsoever or any tradition or anything that tells the court what to do if a former owner comes in and says, I'd like to get my property back, and the state says, well, I'd rather not because we've got somebody willing to pay a million dollars for it? But what is the court supposed to do? Mr. Justice Stevens, if the petition is made by the former owner to the deputy commissioner's office in each county, that deputy commissioner has forms printed up that he will supply to the landowner, and it doesn't even take a counsel. Usually he will get counsel because by then he has seen what difficult straits he is in. But there is a form petition and a form order, and just as a pro-forma proceeding, the former owner is allowed to redeem under the control of the local circuit court. Well, then is this somewhat analogous to the situation where a discharged schoolteacher didn't have a contract but had an expectancy that he'd always get relief if he went in and asked for it? There's no statutory right to recovery, but the practice is so clear and definite that she would always win if she got notice. So why isn't there the same need for notice as if she had a legal right to the property? Because the apparent value of the asset at the time it is sold simply will not bear the expense of determining the names and the addresses of the parties that need the notice, if you determine that they need notice. The state of West Virginia faced up to this, and during the Depression years, they had a chancery proceeding in West Virginia where you served in these suits, personal service on the residents and publication against the non-residents, but the title searches by the deputy commissioners were costing so much money that it obsoleted the value of the sale. Mr. Rice, may we go back to the original notice? The tax we're talking about was due for the year 1961. When did the property owner or the owner of this interest receive the tax bill for 1960? Your Honor, that needs some clarification. Never. Well, I understand that, but when are these bills sent out? They are not in West Virginia until 1976. There is a recent enactment. You referred to a tax ticket, I think. There is a tax ticket, but the owner or the interested person has to go ultimately and pick up the tax ticket. There was no tax bill, in other words. No, there is a tax bill, but it is not sent. It's not sent to anybody. You have to go get it. So Mr. Pearson Sr. went to the courthouse and picked up the tax ticket every year? For 24 years he did. And then nobody went. They could have gone in 1961. They could have gone in 62. They could have gone in 63. Well, the property belonged to the state after 62. But they still could have... Well, the 18 months didn't run until 1964. The middle of 1964. Well, I take it that even if the... Even if the... Even if on the tax records the name of the true owner had appeared, the same thing would have happened here. There would have been no notice. There would have been publication. There would have been publication, but there would have been no personal notice. No personal notice. The state's brief tells us that she could have redeemed up to May 27, 1966. Do you agree with that date? No, I do not agree with that date. What date would... It's taken the four years and added 18 months to it. May of 1966, did you say? Yes. Your Honor, that date would be accurate then because by then the circuit court suit had started in which it was the state of West Virginia versus all of these unknown owners. And there was a new statutory entitlement that we had denominated where she could have redeemed again. That was the second transaction. That's the second transaction. Mr. Rice, let me give you one more question that troubles me. I'm learning a great deal about this now. In 1962, you say the personal notice is justified if there's a private purchaser but not if the state is doing it because the existence of the private purchaser kind of indicates there's value there and it's worth spending the money to get the... And that purchaser will pursue it. But why isn't the same rationale applicable when the sale is made after the 18 months goes by? Because at that time, you did have a private purchaser and you had a proceeding started. Why wouldn't there be the same reason then to believe there's enough money in the property to support that kind of investment and giving a fair notice to the former owner? After the... Your Honor, after the 18-month period has gone by, that would take you up to roughly 1964. Which would mean there's more back taxes to pay to acquire title, isn't it? Yes, with interest. Right. Then you... Then you... It's only in 1966 that you have this second suit by the state of West Virginia against the... What I say is an in-rim proceeding. By that time, it's your submission, I suppose, that the state of West Virginia has been the owner of the fee title for several years. That was what the holding below was. But at that time, you're willing to expend the money to have a judicial proceeding, but you're not willing to spend that little more amount to get service on the former owner, which you would have spent before.
